## 1. The question and the experiment

Two friends agree to meet at a reference time $t=0$. Each arrives during the following hour. Whoever arrives first waits for 15 minutes, then leaves if the other has not arrived. **What is the probability that they do not meet?**

This student-raised problem lets us distinguish a set of outcomes from the probability assigned to it. We will solve the same question under two stipulated arrival models: independent uniform arrivals, and independent arrivals with a density that decreases over the hour. Neither is claimed to describe observed arrival behavior.

We assume each friend does arrive within the hour, the first arrival waits the full 15 minutes even if that extends beyond the hour, and arrival exactly at the departure time counts as a meeting. The boundary convention does not affect probabilities under the two density models below.

### Identify the probability objects

Measure time in hours. An outcome is the ordered pair $\omega=(t_A,t_B)$: A's arrival time first, B's second. For example, $(0.2,0.3)$ means A arrives after 12 minutes and B after 18 minutes; they meet because the gap is six minutes.

Take

$$\Omega=[0,1]^2,\qquad \mathcal F=\mathcal B([0,1]^2).$$

The Borel sigma-algebra includes the rectangles, triangles and diagonal bands used here. Define the coordinate random variables

$$T_A(t_A,t_B)=t_A,\qquad T_B(t_A,t_B)=t_B.$$

The triplet is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, but the specification is incomplete until we choose $P$. A joint density will assign probabilities to events by integration.

## 2. Describe the event before choosing a density

The waiting allowance is $\delta=15/60=1/4$ hour. The friends meet precisely when their arrival-time difference is at most $\delta$:

$$M_\delta=\{\omega:|T_A(\omega)-T_B(\omega)|\le\delta\}.$$

Its complement, the event asked for, is

$$N_\delta=\{\omega:|T_A(\omega)-T_B(\omega)|>\delta\}.$$

Split the no-meeting event into two disjoint possibilities:

$$N_\delta=\{T_B>T_A+\delta\}\ \cup\ \{T_A>T_B+\delta\}.$$

In the first, B arrives too late for A; in the second, A arrives too late for B. On the unit square with $t_A$ horizontal and $t_B$ vertical, the meeting event is the band between $t_B=t_A-\delta$ and $t_B=t_A+\delta$. The two remaining corner triangles form $N_\delta$. These are measurable regions, so $P$ can act on them.

**Before calculating:** sketch the unit square and locate $(0.2,0.3)$ and $(0.1,0.8)$. Decide which belongs to the meeting band. The model has not yet told us whether area alone gives probability.

[Open the waiting-time demonstration](../materials/02-random-variables/meeting-problem.html). Both panels use the same square and meeting band. Their background shading represents different joint densities.

## 3. Model U: independent uniform arrivals

### Specify the measure

Assume $T_A$ and $T_B$ are independent and each uniform on $[0,1]$. Their marginal densities are 1 on that interval, zero elsewhere. Independence gives

$$f_U(t_A,t_B)=\begin{cases}1,&(t_A,t_B)\in[0,1]^2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

For a Borel event $E\subseteq\Omega$,

$$P_U(E)=\iint_E1\,dt_A\,dt_B.$$

This integrates to 1 on the square. Under this particular measure, probability equals area. Merely specifying the square would not justify equal area weights.

### Geometry first: probability of not meeting

At $\delta=1/4$, each no-meeting triangle has two perpendicular sides of length $1-\delta=3/4$. Its area is

$$\frac12\left(\frac34\right)^2=\frac9{32}.$$

The triangles are disjoint, so

$$P_U(N_{1/4})=2\left(\frac9{32}\right)=\boxed{\frac9{16}=0.5625}.$$

Consequently,

$$P_U(M_{1/4})=1-\frac9{16}=\boxed{\frac7{16}=0.4375}.$$

The answer to the original no-meeting question is **56.25% under independent uniform arrivals**.

### Recover the result by a double integral

For the upper triangle, $0\le t_A<3/4$ and $t_A+1/4<t_B\le1$. Symmetry of this joint density under exchanging the friends gives equal probabilities to the two triangles:

$$\begin{aligned}
P_U(N_{1/4})
&=2\int_0^{3/4}\int_{t_A+1/4}^1 1\,dt_B\,dt_A\\
&=2\int_0^{3/4}\left(\frac34-t_A\right)dt_A\\
&=2\left[\frac34t_A-\frac{t_A^2}{2}\right]_0^{3/4}
=\frac9{16}.
\end{aligned}$$

Integration adds density over the original event, just as a finite probability model adds outcome weights. The factor of 2 uses symmetry; independence alone would not justify it if the two arrival distributions differed.

**Suggested stopping point.** Have learners explain the integration bounds and why the two triangles have equal probabilities before changing the arrival model.

## 4. Model E: independent arrivals weighted toward earlier times

### Normalize the proposed marginal density

Keep the same experiment and waiting rule. Now stipulate that each arrival has density proportional to $1-t$ on $[0,1]$. With $f_T(t)=c(1-t)$ there,

$$1=\int_0^1c(1-t)\,dt=c\left[t-\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\frac c2,$$

so

$$f_T(t)=\begin{cases}2(1-t),&0\le t\le1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

This is a different hypothetical model, not a conclusion that these friends actually arrive early. A higher density near zero means an interval of fixed small length near zero receives more probability than one near the end of the hour. A single exact time still has probability zero.

For example,

$$P_E(T_A\le1/4)=\int_0^{1/4}2(1-t)\,dt
=\left[2t-t^2\right]_0^{1/4}=\frac7{16},$$

compared with $1/4$ in Model U.

### Independence still holds, but the measure changes

Assume the two arrivals are independent with this same marginal density. The joint density is

$$f_E(t_A,t_B)=4(1-t_A)(1-t_B)\quad\text{on }[0,1]^2,$$

and zero elsewhere. It integrates to 1 because each marginal integrates to 1. The probability measure is now

$$P_E(E)=\iint_E4(1-t_A)(1-t_B)\,dt_A\,dt_B.$$

The outcome space, sigma-algebra, coordinate functions and meeting event are unchanged. Only the probability measure changes. Probability is no longer the unweighted area of a region.

### Integrate over the same two triangles

The density remains symmetric in $t_A,t_B$. Hence

$$P_E(N_{1/4})=2\int_0^{3/4}\int_{t_A+1/4}^1
4(1-t_A)(1-t_B)\,dt_B\,dt_A.$$

For a fixed $t_A$,

$$\int_{t_A+1/4}^1(1-t_B)\,dt_B
=\frac12\left(\frac34-t_A\right)^2.$$

Thus

$$P_E(N_{1/4})=4\int_0^{3/4}(1-t_A)\left(\frac34-t_A\right)^2dt_A.$$

To show the remaining arithmetic, put $u=3/4-t_A$, so $1-t_A=1/4+u$:

$$\begin{aligned}
P_E(N_{1/4})
&=4\int_0^{3/4}\left(\frac14+u\right)u^2\,du\\
&=4\left[\frac{u^3}{12}+\frac{u^4}{4}\right]_0^{3/4}\\
&=\frac9{64}+\frac{81}{256}
=\boxed{\frac{117}{256}\approx0.45703125}.
\end{aligned}$$

Therefore

$$P_E(M_{1/4})=1-\frac{117}{256}=\boxed{\frac{139}{256}\approx0.54296875}.$$

| Arrival model | Meet within the waiting allowance | Do not meet |
|---|---:|---:|
| Independent uniform | $7/16=43.75\%$ | $9/16=56.25\%$ |
| Independent decreasing-density | $139/256\approx54.30\%$ | $117/256\approx45.70\%$ |

Both models assume independent arrivals. In this comparison, changing both marginal densities increases the probability that the two times are close. Independence does not fix the meeting probability. Nor does the calculation prove that every possible model favoring early arrivals must improve it.

## 5. Transform the pair into an arrival-time gap

### A one-dimensional variable for the same question

Define the measurable function $g(t_A,t_B)=|t_A-t_B|$ and the random variable

$$D=g(T_A,T_B)=|T_A-T_B|.$$

Its values are gaps in hours, from 0 to 1. The meeting event is the inverse image

$$M_\delta=D^{-1}([0,\delta])=\{D\le\delta\}.$$

Many arrival pairs have the same gap. Thus the distribution of $D$ retains the gap information and discards the individual arrival times. It is induced by the original measure: for a Borel set $B$ of gaps, $P_D(B)=P(D^{-1}(B))$.

### Derive the gap CDF and PDF under uniform arrivals

For $0\le d\le1$, the two triangles outside the band of width $d$ have total area $(1-d)^2$. Hence the **CDF**, defined by $F_{D,U}(d)=P_U(D\le d)$, is

$$F_{D,U}(d)=\begin{cases}
0,&d<0,\\
1-(1-d)^2=2d-d^2,&0\le d\le1,\\
1,&d>1.
\end{cases}$$

Differentiating on $(0,1)$ gives a **PDF**:

$$f_{D,U}(d)=2(1-d)\quad(0<d<1),$$

zero outside $[0,1]$. Its values at the endpoints do not affect any probability. It is nonnegative and integrates to 1. Recover the meeting probability:

$$P_U(D\le1/4)=\int_0^{1/4}2(1-d)\,dd
=\left[2d-d^2\right]_0^{1/4}=\frac7{16}.$$

This density has the same formula as the **individual arrival-time density in Model E**, but it describes a different variable under a different probability measure. In Model E, the gap density is not $2(1-d)$.

## 6. Vary the waiting policy, retaining the models

Let $w$ be the waiting allowance in minutes and $\delta=w/60$. For $0\le\delta\le1$, the uniform calculation gives

$$P_U(N_\delta)=(1-\delta)^2,\qquad
P_U(M_\delta)=2\delta-\delta^2.$$

In Model E, the same integration with $1/4$ replaced by $\delta$ gives, with $a=1-\delta$,

$$\begin{aligned}
P_E(N_\delta)
&=4\int_0^{1-\delta}(1-t)(1-\delta-t)^2\,dt\\
&=4\int_0^a(\delta+u)u^2\,du
=\frac{4\delta a^3}{3}+a^4\\
&=(1-\delta)^3\left(1+\frac\delta3\right).
\end{aligned}$$

Therefore

$$P_E(M_\delta)=1-(1-\delta)^3\left(1+\frac\delta3\right).$$

At zero waiting time, meeting requires equal arrival times, a diagonal of probability zero under both models. At 60 minutes, all pairs qualify and the meeting probability is 1. Increasing the waiting allowance enlarges the event without changing either model's measure.

[Explore waiting times from 0 to 60 minutes](../materials/02-random-variables/meeting-problem.html). The demonstration evaluates these formulas exactly up to numerical rounding; its shaded grid is only a display of density, not a numerical probability estimator.

**Practice check 1.** If the waiting allowance rises from 15 to 30 minutes, does the meeting probability double? Calculate the result under each model and explain using the expanded band.

**Practice check 2.** Under uniform arrivals, what waiting allowance is needed for a meeting probability of at least $3/4$? State your answer in minutes.

**Practice check 3.** Keep uniform marginal arrivals but suppose $T_B=T_A$ exactly. What is the meeting probability at zero waiting time? Explain which original assumption fails and why a two-dimensional joint PDF no longer describes this new model.

## 7. What stays fixed and what changes?

| Object | In this example |
|---|---|
| Outcome $\omega$ | An ordered pair of arrival times |
| Sample space $\Omega$ | The unit square |
| Event collection $\mathcal F$ | Its Borel sigma-algebra |
| Random variables $T_A,T_B$ | Coordinate projections |
| Transformed variable $D$ | The absolute arrival-time gap |
| Event $M_\delta$ | The inverse-image band $D^{-1}([0,\delta])$ |
| Probability measure | $P_U$ or $P_E$, defined by its joint density |
| Probability of meeting | The integral of the chosen density over the band |

Changing the arrival density changes the measure while leaving a fixed waiting-time event unchanged. Changing the waiting allowance changes the event while leaving a chosen arrival model unchanged. The [supplement](02-random-variables-supplement.qmd#meeting-time-transformation) derives the gap density under both models and states the independence and density assumptions needed for that calculation.

## Appendix A · From joint arrivals to the actual waiting-time distribution {#waiting-time-appendix}

### A.1. Questions, assumptions and notation

If the friends arrive 40 minutes apart, the first friend waits only 15 minutes before leaving. The arrival gap and the actual waiting time therefore answer different questions. In this appendix we derive the distributions of both, then calculate the mean and variance of the actual wait.

The learning sequence is to construct the joint density, define a function of the pair, calculate its CDF from an event region, differentiate when a density exists, apply a second transformation, identify any resulting point mass, and calculate moments using the complete law.

We use **Model U only**: the two arrivals are independent and uniform during the hour following $t=0$. Each friend does arrive within that hour. The first friend waits up to 15 minutes even if that extends beyond the end of the arrival window. Arrival exactly at the departure time counts as a meeting; this equality has probability zero in the stipulated model.

To remain consistent with the rest of this course, we write

$$D=|T_A-T_B|\quad\text{for the arrival gap},\qquad
W=\min(D,1/4)\quad\text{for the actual wait}.$$

All formula arguments below are in **hours**, unless stated otherwise. $W$ records the wait of whichever friend arrives first, not the wait of a particular named friend or the sum of both friends' waits. At a simultaneous arrival, define the wait as zero.

[Open the interactive CDF, density and point-mass demonstration](../materials/02-random-variables/meeting-waiting-distributions.html). Start at a 15-minute cap and compare the CDF immediately below the cap with its value at the cap. Then change the waiting policy.

### A.2. Construct the probability triplet and joint law

An outcome is an ordered pair $\omega=(t_A,t_B)$. The probability model is

$$\Omega=[0,1]^2,\qquad\mathcal F=\mathcal B([0,1]^2),\qquad
P_U(E)=\iint_E1\,dt_A\,dt_B\quad(E\in\mathcal F).$$

The coordinate variables $T_A(\omega)=t_A$ and $T_B(\omega)=t_B$ each have density 1 on $[0,1]$, zero elsewhere. Independence gives

$$f_{T_A,T_B}(t_A,t_B)=
\begin{cases}1,&(t_A,t_B)\in[0,1]^2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

Thus $P_U(E)=\operatorname{Area}(E)$ for Borel regions in the square. Equal probability per unit area is a property of this measure; it does not follow merely from choosing a square sample space. Individual points have probability zero, so “uniform” means equal-length arrival intervals have equal probabilities, not positive equal probabilities assigned to individual arrival times.

An outcome is one pair; an event is a measurable set of pairs; a random variable maps each pair to a number. All subsequent transformations use this same probability triplet.

### A.3. First transformation: the gap between arrival times

Define $D(\omega)=|T_A(\omega)-T_B(\omega)|$. This is a measurable function with range $[0,1]$. It is deterministic given the arrivals, but random before the outcome is known.

| A's arrival (hours) | B's arrival (hours) | Gap $D$ (hours) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.10 |
| 0.30 | 0.80 | 0.50 |
| 0.70 | 0.70 | 0 |
| 0.90 | 0.60 | 0.30 |

For a real threshold $d$, the **CDF** is $F_D(d)=P_U(D\le d)$. When $0\le d\le1$,

$$\begin{aligned}
\{D\le d\}
&=\{|T_A-T_B|\le d\}\\
&=\{-d\le T_A-T_B\le d\}\\
&=\{T_A-d\le T_B\le T_A+d\}.
\end{aligned}$$

The inverse image of $[0,d]$ is the diagonal band between $t_B=t_A-d$ and $t_B=t_A+d$. Each excluded corner triangle has perpendicular sides of length $1-d$. Their total area is $2[\tfrac12(1-d)^2]=(1-d)^2$. Therefore

$$F_D(d)=1-(1-d)^2=2d-d^2\qquad(0\le d\le1).$$

The integration limits give the same result. For the upper excluded triangle, $0\le t_A<1-d$ and $t_A+d<t_B\le1$:

$$\begin{aligned}
P_U(D>d)
&=2\int_0^{1-d}\int_{t_A+d}^1 1\,dt_B\,dt_A\\
&=2\int_0^{1-d}(1-d-t_A)\,dt_A\\
&=2\left[(1-d)t_A-\frac{t_A^2}{2}\right]_0^{1-d}
=(1-d)^2.
\end{aligned}$$

The factor of 2 is justified by the symmetry of this joint law. Include thresholds outside the range to obtain

$$\boxed{F_D(d)=\begin{cases}
0,&d<0,\\
2d-d^2,&0\le d\le1,\\
1,&d>1.
\end{cases}}$$

This CDF is absolutely continuous. Its derivative gives a density, up to choices at endpoints:

$$f_D(d)=\begin{cases}2(1-d),&0<d<1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

Check normalization: $\int_0^1 2(1-d)\,dd=[2d-d^2]_0^1=1$. The gap is not uniform even though both inputs are uniform. Intervals of a given small length near zero receive more gap probability than intervals of that length near one hour. This statement compares intervals, not positive probabilities at individual points.

A CDF always exists for a real random variable. Differentiation recovers the full law as a PDF when the CDF is absolutely continuous; a continuous CDF alone is not a sufficient condition in complete generality.

### A.4. Use the gap distribution to answer the meeting question

A 15-minute cap is $1/4$ hour. The meeting event is $M_{1/4}=\{D\le1/4\}$. Consequently,

$$\begin{aligned}
P_U(M_{1/4})&=F_D(1/4)
=2\left(\frac14\right)-\left(\frac14\right)^2\\
&=\frac12-\frac1{16}=\boxed{\frac7{16}=43.75\%}.
\end{aligned}$$

The probability of no meeting is $1-7/16=9/16$. This uses the distribution of the uncapped gap, not a distribution of actual waiting times.

### A.5. Second transformation: cap the wait

The first arrival waits until the second arrives or the allowance expires:

$$W=\min(D,1/4)=\min(|T_A-T_B|,1/4).$$

| Arrival gap | Actual wait |
|---|---|
| 0.05 hour = 3 minutes | 3 minutes |
| 0.10 hour = 6 minutes | 6 minutes |
| 0.20 hour = 12 minutes | 12 minutes |
| 0.40 hour = 24 minutes | 15 minutes |
| 0.80 hour = 48 minutes | 15 minutes |

Equivalently,

$$W=\begin{cases}D,&0\le D<1/4,\\1/4,&D\ge1/4.\end{cases}$$

The composition $(T_A,T_B)\mapsto D\mapsto W$ changes the recorded quantity without changing the original probability measure. The range of $W$ is $[0,1/4]$.

### A.6. Derive the waiting-time CDF in three cases

Start from $F_W(w)=P_U(W\le w)$.

**Case 1: $w<0$.** A wait cannot be negative, so $F_W(w)=0$.

**Case 2: $0\le w<1/4$.** Because the cap exceeds the threshold,

$$\{\min(D,1/4)\le w\}=\{D\le w\}.$$

To check both directions: if $D\le w$, the minimum is at most $w$; if $D>w$, both $D$ and $1/4$ exceed $w$, so their minimum also exceeds $w$. Hence

$$F_W(w)=F_D(w)=2w-w^2.$$

**Case 3: $w\ge1/4$.** Every possible wait is at most $1/4$, so the event is all of $\Omega$ and $F_W(w)=1$.

Combining the cases,

$$\boxed{F_W(w)=\begin{cases}
0,&w<0,\\
2w-w^2,&0\le w<1/4,\\
1,&w\ge1/4.
\end{cases}}$$

The middle interval excludes $1/4$. At that threshold the event suddenly includes all the outcomes whose waits were capped.

### A.7. Interpret the jump at 15 minutes

The left-hand limit and the value at the cap are

$$F_W(1/4^-)=\frac7{16},\qquad F_W(1/4)=1.$$

For any CDF, a jump at $a$ has size $P(W=a)=F_W(a)-F_W(a^-)$. Here,

$$\boxed{P_U(W=1/4)=1-\frac7{16}=\frac9{16}.}$$

The transformation sends the whole set $\{D\ge1/4\}$ to the one value $1/4$. Although $P_U(D=1/4)=0$, the larger event $\{D\ge1/4\}$ has probability $9/16$. A transformation can therefore create a point mass by mapping a positive-probability set onto a single value.

In the visualization, the open point at height $7/16$ marks the left limit. The filled point at height 1 marks the CDF value at the cap. The vertical connector indicates the jump; it does not mean the function takes intermediate values at $w=1/4$. The CDF is right-continuous.

### A.8. Specify the complete mixed distribution

Differentiating below the cap gives the **continuous component density**

$$f_{W,\mathrm{ac}}(w)=2(1-w)\,\mathbf1_{(0,1/4)}(w).$$

This is not a normalized PDF for the whole law:

$$\int_0^{1/4}2(1-w)\,dw=\frac7{16}.$$

The remaining $9/16$ is an atom at $1/4$. For any Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, a complete specification is

$$\boxed{P_U(W\in B)=\int_{B\cap(0,1/4)}2(1-w)\,dw
+\frac9{16}\mathbf1_{\{1/4\in B\}}.}$$

The integral and point mass sum to $7/16+9/16=1$. Thus the law is **mixed**, with a continuous component and a discrete component. There is no ordinary density with respect to length that represents all its probability.

One may write the law as $f_{W,\mathrm{ac}}(w)\,dw+(9/16)\delta_{1/4}(dw)$, where $\delta_{1/4}$ is the unit point-mass measure at $1/4$. This notation does not treat a Dirac mass as a finite-height PDF value. The visualization therefore shows the continuous density and the atom on separate, labelled scales.

**Suggested stopping point.** Ask students to explain why $P(D=1/4)=0$ and $P(W=1/4)=9/16$ can both hold before calculating moments.

### A.9. Mean waiting time: include both components

Expectation is the probability-weighted mean. For the complete mixed law,

$$E[W]=\int_0^{1/4}w\,2(1-w)\,dw+\frac14\frac9{16}.$$

The integral accounts for waits below 15 minutes; the second term accounts for the full-cap waits. Compute each contribution:

$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{1/4}w\,2(1-w)\,dw
&=2\int_0^{1/4}(w-w^2)\,dw\\
&=\left[w^2-\frac{2w^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/4}
=\frac1{16}-\frac1{96}=\frac5{96},\\
\frac14\frac9{16}&=\frac9{64}.
\end{aligned}$$

Therefore

$$E[W]=\frac5{96}+\frac9{64}
=\frac{10+27}{192}=\boxed{\frac{37}{192}\text{ hour}}.$$

With $W_m=60W$ in minutes, linearity gives

$$\boxed{E[W_m]=60\frac{37}{192}=11.5625\text{ minutes}.}$$

Under independent repetitions of the stated experiment, the sample average converges to this expectation. The result includes both successful and unsuccessful meetings; it is not the conditional mean among pairs who meet. It also differs from $E[D]$, since a gap above 15 minutes is not fully spent waiting.

### A.10. Second moment, variance and standard deviation

The variance is the expected squared deviation from the mean:

$$\operatorname{Var}(W)=E[(W-E[W])^2]=E[W^2]-(E[W])^2.$$

First calculate the second moment using both components:

$$\begin{aligned}
E[W^2]
&=\int_0^{1/4}w^2\,2(1-w)\,dw+\left(\frac14\right)^2\frac9{16}\\
&=\left[\frac{2w^3}{3}-\frac{w^4}{2}\right]_0^{1/4}+\frac9{256}\\
&=\frac1{96}-\frac1{512}+\frac9{256}\\
&=\frac{16-3+54}{1536}
=\boxed{\frac{67}{1536}\text{ hours}^2}.
\end{aligned}$$

Now subtract the square of the mean, using a common denominator:

$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(W)
&=\frac{67}{1536}-\left(\frac{37}{192}\right)^2\\
&=\frac{1608-1369}{36864}
=\boxed{\frac{239}{36864}\text{ hours}^2}
\approx0.00648329\text{ hours}^2.
\end{aligned}$$

Changing units multiplies variance by the **square** of the conversion factor:

$$\operatorname{Var}(W_m)=60^2\operatorname{Var}(W)
=\frac{5975}{256}=\boxed{23.33984375\text{ minutes}^2}.$$

The standard deviation returns to the original units:

$$\operatorname{SD}(W_m)=\sqrt{23.33984375}\approx\boxed{4.831\text{ minutes}}.$$

The second moment $E[W^2]$ and the variance are different quantities. Ignoring the point mass would give incorrect values for both the mean and the second moment.

### A.11. Recalculate through survival probabilities

For a nonnegative random variable $V$,

$$E[V]=\int_0^\infty P(V>t)\,dt.$$

To see why, write each nonnegative value as its accumulated indicators: $V(\omega)=\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{V(\omega)>t\}}dt$. Interchange the two nonnegative integrals to obtain the formula. Likewise, $V(\omega)^2=\int_0^\infty2t\mathbf1_{\{V(\omega)>t\}}dt$ gives

$$E[V^2]=2\int_0^\infty tP(V>t)\,dt.$$

These identities apply to nonnegative continuous, discrete and mixed laws, with infinite expectations allowed. Here $W$ is bounded, so the moments are finite.

For $0\le t<1/4$, $\{W>t\}=\{D>t\}$ and

$$P_U(W>t)=1-F_D(t)=(1-t)^2.$$

For $t\ge1/4$, it is zero. Therefore

$$\begin{aligned}
E[W]&=\int_0^{1/4}(1-t)^2dt\\
&=\left[t-t^2+\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/4}
=\frac14-\frac1{16}+\frac1{192}=\frac{37}{192},\\
E[W^2]&=2\int_0^{1/4}t(1-t)^2dt\\
&=\left[t^2-\frac{4t^3}{3}+\frac{t^4}{2}\right]_0^{1/4}
=\frac1{16}-\frac1{48}+\frac1{512}=\frac{67}{1536}.
\end{aligned}$$

The survival function falls from a left limit $9/16$ to 0 at the cap. Its value at that one integration endpoint does not change either integral. No extra atom term is needed in this method: the full-cap outcomes contribute to $P(W>t)$ at every threshold below the cap.

### A.12. Consolidate the objects and results

| Object | Function of the original outcome | Law under Model U |
|---|---|---|
| $T_A$ | First coordinate $t_A$ | Uniform on $[0,1]$ |
| $T_B$ | Second coordinate $t_B$ | Uniform on $[0,1]$ |
| $(T_A,T_B)$ | The pair $(t_A,t_B)$ | Density 1 on the unit square |
| $D$ | $|t_A-t_B|$ | Density $2(1-d)$ on $(0,1)$ |
| $W$ | $\min(|t_A-t_B|,1/4)$ | Continuous component below $1/4$ and atom at $1/4$ |

| Quantity | Result |
|---|---|
| Meeting probability | $7/16=43.75\%$ |
| Probability of a full 15-minute wait | $9/16=56.25\%$ |
| Mean actual wait | $37/192$ hour = 11.5625 minutes |
| Second moment of actual wait | $67/1536$ hours squared |
| Variance of actual wait | $239/36864$ hours squared = 23.33984375 minutes squared |
| Standard deviation of actual wait | Approximately 4.831 minutes |

The two full-cap and no-meeting events differ only by $\{D=1/4\}$, a null event here. That explains their equal probabilities without asserting that meeting at exactly the cap is impossible as an outcome.

For another cap $a$, the same procedure uses the event $\{\min(D,a)\le w\}$, splits the law into the continuous component below $a$ and its mass at $a$, and computes moments from the complete law. The accompanying sliders keep the independent uniform arrival measure fixed while changing this policy. Similar calculations describe capped losses or a sensor reading limited by a display ceiling. Capping keeps the affected outcomes and records the limit; it is different from discarding observations above a threshold.

### A.13. Independent exercises

**A1. A 30-minute allowance.** Define $W=\min(D,1/2)$. Construct its CDF, specify its continuous component and point mass, and calculate its mean. State the units of your answer.

**A2. A general allowance.** For $0<a<1$, define $W_a=\min(D,a)$. Derive the mass at $a$, the first and second moments, and the variance as functions of $a$. Check their limits as $a\downarrow0$ and $a\uparrow1$.

**A3. Uncapped versus capped.** Calculate the mean and variance of the gap $D$, and compare them with those of $W=\min(D,1/4)$. Use the transformations to explain the changes; keep hours and minutes consistent.

**A4. Conditional waiting.** Given that the friends meet, calculate $E[W\mid D\le1/4]$. Identify the conditioning probability, normalize the restricted law, and explain why the result differs from the unconditional mean.

**A5. Simulation.** Generate 10,000 independent pairs $(T_{A,i},T_{B,i})$ with independent uniform coordinates. Record $D_i=|T_{A,i}-T_{B,i}|$ and $W_i=\min(D_i,1/4)$. Estimate the meeting probability, the full-cap frequency, the mean wait and its variance. State your seed and whether the variance calculation uses denominator $n$ or $n-1$. Compare with the analytic results and explain why finite-sample estimates need not agree exactly. When plotting, show the atom separately instead of interpreting a histogram spike as an ordinary PDF height.

For the general theory behind the moment calculations, see [01.5: expectation and variance](05-expectation-variance.qmd). For inverse images, Jacobians and mixed transformed laws, see [01.6: transformations](06-transformations.qmd). The [distribution-theory supplement](02-random-variables-supplement.qmd#meeting-time-transformation) derives the uncapped gap density for both arrival models.
